To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) influenza super-strains are capable of sustaining epidemics in human populations even when the transmissibility in humans is low and (2) the dynamics of influenza epidemics in human population can be predicted by three factors (i.e., transmissibility in human, transmissibility from pig to humans, and contact between humans and pigs).

(1) the epidemiology of influenza super-strain outbreaks depends on the contact between pigs and human, (2) super-strain outbreaks will occur if the super-strain transmits well in humans, (3) the super-strain will be more likely to persist if it can be transmitted from pigs to humans and (4) super-strains that caused past epidemics could reemerge
(1) the emergence of a novel strain is necessary but not sufficient for an outbreak and (2) the transmissibility from humans to humans is not the only factor in the outbreak.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epidemiological dynamics of influenza and the potential of super-strains to cause pandemics in the future.
the epidemiology of super-strain emergence and dynamics and provides insights into the role of species interactions in the emergence of new pathogens
the emergence of new super-strains and their potential to generate major outbreaks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the epidemiological outcome of emergent influenza super-strains will depend on the transmissibility in humans and between humans and pigs.

a super-strain that is capable of sustaining epidemics is likely to emerge, and the dynamics of the outbreak will depend on the transmissibility between humans and pigs and the transmissibility in humans.
the emergence of a super-strains does not necessarily lead to an outbreak.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, the emergence of super-strains in the pig population can be an important step in the evolution of influenza viruses.
the emergence and spread of a super-strains is not only dependent on the transmissibility in humans but also dependent on transmissibility between pigs and humans and between pigs and birds.
super-strains that emerge in pigs are not always capable of causing major epidemics in humans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dynamics of influenza are not only determined by the transmissibility between hosts, but also the interactions between species.
the emergence of a new influenza strain does not always guarantee a pandemic.
the epidemiology of influenza super-strain infections is highly dependent on the contact between humans and pigs.
